input:
This pricing case takes a detailed look at a catering contract in order to establish the volume at which the contract in question breaks even, and how that particular volume compares with the volume that is currently being achieved. The contract is priced at $157 per unit, while the variable cost comes in at $82 per unit, which means that each unit that is sold makes a contribution of $75 per unit towards the fixed costs of the business. Those fixed costs amount to $108k per year, and dividing them by the contribution per unit gives a break-even volume of 1440 units per year. The current volume, by way of comparison, is running at 1872 units per year, so the contract is currently trading comfortably above the volume at which it breaks even, at least on the face of the figures.

It is important to bear in mind, however, that there are a couple of caveats that really do need to be kept in view here. In the first place, the volume figures that have been used are last year's actuals, so the comfortable margin that appears above break-even is essentially a statement about how last year actually turned out rather than any kind of forecast of the year that lies ahead. In the second place, the effect that the price itself has on the volume has not been estimated anywhere in this analysis, which means that the calculation simply holds the volume fixed at the level that was actually delivered and cannot really say what volume a different price might bring in. A higher price could quite plausibly reduce the volume, and the contract could move closer to break-even even at the very same time as the contribution per unit was rising.
target:
The catering contract breaks even at 1440 units per year. Current volume is 1872 units per year, so on last year's figures the contract trades above its break-even volume. The price is $157 per unit and the variable cost is $82 per unit, which gives a contribution of $75 per unit. Fixed costs are $108k per year, and the break-even volume is the fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit: the volume at which the contribution from the units sold exactly covers the fixed costs of the year. Volume above that level contributes at the rate of the contribution on each further unit sold, and volume below it leaves part of the fixed costs uncovered by the trading of the year.

Two limits bound the finding, and both stand on the volume side of the case. The volume figures are last year's actuals, so the margin above break-even is a statement about last year's trading and not a forecast of the year ahead; a contract priced on these figures carries last year's volume as an assumption built into the price. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated. The calculation holds the volume fixed at the level actually delivered and varies nothing else, so the calculation cannot say what volume a different price would bring. A price rise that cost volume could move the contract towards break-even even as the contribution per unit rose. What the figures establish is narrower than a pricing recommendation: at the present price and at last year's volume, the contract covers its fixed costs with volume to spare, and the size of that spare volume is the measure of the case.
